newsitem.title: USA: U.S. inflation slack in January but trade gap jumps.
newsitem.headline: U.S. inflation slack in January but trade gap jumps.

text.p: Consumers got more good news Wednesday when the government reported that inflation remained in check in January as the economy approached its sixth anniversary of steady growth.

The vibrant U.S. economy also had a downside, however, as the surging dollar helped attract a swelling volume of imported goods that pushed the country's annual trade deficit with other nations to the highest level in almost a decade.

The Labour Department reported that the Consumer Price Index, one of the key measures of inflation, rose only 0.1 percent last month -- its smallest monthly gain since last summer -- after a 0.3 percent increase in December.
Separately, the Commerce Department said the shortfall on trade with the rest of the world shot up in December by 29.6 percent to $10.29 billion from a revised $7.94 billion in November.
As a result, the total gap on goods and services trade in 1996 climbed 8.7 percent from 1995 to $114.23 billion -- the highest red-ink total since $115.5 billion in 1988.

Deteriorating world trade ironically underlined the good news on the domestic inflation front. The economy is nearing a sixth anniversary of unbroken growth next month, from the last recession in 1990-1991, on a wave of imports.

The U.S. economy, generating strong job and income growth, has been drawing in foreign-made goods as traditional European powerhouses like Germany languish and Asian giants Japan and China concentrate on boosting their exports.
Despite buoyant consumer demand, food prices took their sharpest drop in 3-1/2 years during January, offsetting a moderate increase in energy prices, including gasoline.

Last month's rate of price rises was even lower than analysts had anticipated. It heartened financial markets briefly because low inflation reduces chances that Federal Reserve policy-makers might soon raise interest rates to keep prices under control.
"This is virtually no inflation at all," said Philip Braverman, chief economist at DKB Securities Inc., on Reuters Financial Television.

Even with volatile food and energy sectors left out, the so-called core rate of price rises, which analysts say more closely tracks inflation over the longer term, still rose just 0.1 percent after rising 0.2 percent in December.
Medical costs, a key factor in keeping labour costs under control, also remained largely quiet in January, rising 0.2 percent, the same as a month earlier.
The department said the January's 0.1 percent rise in consumer prices matched the increase last June, while the decline in food prices was the largest since a 0.4 percent drop in June 1993.

The trade report posed potential problems, however, with several analysts claiming that overseas trading partners manipulate policy and exchange rates to gain an unfair advantage against the United States and should be challenged on it.
"Europe and Japan will only develop an increased appetite for American goods when they deregulate their economies," said Howard Lewis, vice president of the National Association of Manufacturers.
Costlier oil and sluggish demand for U.S. goods like food, capital goods and auto parts in Europe and other overseas economies were among the culprits accounting for slacker export trade in December.

Analysts cautioned that the trade deficit likely will worsen in 1997 as the dollar's rising value makes American products more costly for foreigners to buy while imported Japanese cars and Chinese-manufactured clothing becomes relatively cheaper.

However, White House Chief Economist Janet Yellen, a former Federal Reserve governor, said the burgeoning U.S. trade deficit was mainly a result of rising oil prices and oil imports and was not yet a cause for major concern.
"Relative to the size of the economy, the overall deficit (last year) was 1.5 percent, well below the deficits from 1983 to 1989," Yellen said.

But Lawrence Chimerine, chief economist for the Economic Strategy Institute in Washington, said he believed Japan was managing its currency's value for its own advantage and that the overall deficit likely will grow in 1997 to $130 billion or more.

"I think we haven't seen the worst of it yet," Chimerine said. "We haven't seen the full lagged impact of the dollar's rise but we're already seeing Japan taking a large share back of U.S. auto markets."
Overall imports during December grew by 1.5 percent to a record $81.68 billion, while exports declined 1.6 percent to $71.4 billion.
Crude petroleum imports jumped 13.3 percent in value to $4.66 billion in December as the price per barrel increased to $21.65 from $21.44 in November.
The politically sensitive deficit with Japan actually decreased in December by 1.2 percent to $4.27 billion while the gap with China was down 11.7 percent to $2.65 billion.
But the shortfall between exports to China and imports from it for all of 1996 climbed 17 percent to $39.52 billion. That was second only to a $47.68 billion bilateral deficit with Japan.
The trade deficit with Canada soared 32.8 percent to $2.32 billion in December while the gap with Western Europe shot up 48.7 percent to $2.05 billion.
